title: Mini Project
description: Apply Python data analysis skills to solve a real-world data problem from start to finish.
objectives: Pick a dataset and state a question it can answer.
Clean the data and document every decision made.
Produce findings supported by aggregation and charts.
Present the work as a notebook someone else can follow.

slides.title: Mini Project
slides.lead: Everything from Modules 01–05, applied end to end on one dataset of your choice.
bullets: Load — get real data into a DataFrame
Clean — handle missing values, duplicates, and types
Analyze — answer the question with groupby and aggregation
Visualize — three to five charts that carry the findings
Present — a notebook that reads as a report

slides.title: Start with the question
slides.lead: A project without a question produces charts nobody asked for. Write the question in the first markdown cell and keep it visible.
bullets: Good: "Which product category drove the drop in Q2 revenue?"
Weak: "Analyse the sales data"
The question must be answerable from columns you actually have
One main question, at most three supporting ones
Write the answer as a one-sentence hypothesis before you start
slides.note: Datasets to try: Kaggle, data.gov, WHO, World Bank Open Data, or an export from a system you already use.

slides.title: Step 1 — load and look
slides.lead: Before anything else, understand the shape and quality of what you loaded.
slides.note: Keep the raw file untouched in data/raw.csv and write your cleaned version to data/clean.csv. You will want to redo the cleaning at least once.

slides.title: Step 2 — clean, with reasons
slides.lead: Every cleaning decision needs a markdown cell underneath saying why you made it.

body: df["region"] = df["region"].fillna("unknown")    # keep the row, flag the gap
df = df[df["amount"] >= 0]                       # negatives are refunds, out of scope

slides.note: Report how many rows you dropped and why. An analysis that silently discards 40% of the data is not trustworthy.

slides.title: Step 3 — answer the question
slides.lead: Aggregate toward the question you wrote down. Resist exploring columns that cannot answer it.
slides.note: Each aggregation should map to a sentence you can say out loud. If it does not, it does not belong in the report.

slides.title: Step 4 — three to five charts
slides.lead: One chart per finding. More charts than findings means you are showing your process, not your conclusions.
bullets: A trend line for the headline metric over time
A sorted bar chart of the top categories
A distribution or a relationship chart that supports the main claim
Every title states the finding, every axis is labelled
Save each one with fig.savefig(..., dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

slides.title: Step 5 — the notebook as a report
slides.lead: Structure the notebook so a reader who skips every code cell still gets the whole story.
bullets: 1. Question — what you set out to answer and why it matters
2. Data — source, size, date range, and known limitations
3. Cleaning — what you changed, how many rows you lost
4. Findings — one heading per finding, chart directly beneath
5. Conclusion — the answer, plus what you would do with more time
Finish with Kernel ▸ Restart & Run All so it runs top to bottom
slides.note: State the limitations honestly. Naming what your data cannot show makes the parts it does show more credible, not less.

slides.title: Deliverables and marking
slides.lead: Submit these three items. The marking weights tell you where to spend your remaining time.
bullets: project.ipynb — runs clean from a restarted kernel
data/clean.csv and requirements.txt
A 5-minute walkthrough of question, method, and findings
Marking: cleaning 25% · analysis 30% · charts 25% · presentation 20%
slides.note: The most common lost marks: unlabelled charts, no statement of what was dropped during cleaning, and a notebook that fails on restart.

slides.title: Course recap
slides.lead: Six modules, one pipeline you can now run on any dataset you meet.
bullets: 01 — Python foundations: types, functions, containers, files
02 — Environment and the compact syntax of data code
03 — NumPy: vectorised numerical work
04 — Pandas: load, clean, filter, group, join
05 — Matplotlib: charts that make an argument
06 — The whole pipeline, applied and presented
slides.note: Where to go next: statistics for analysts, SQL for pulling your own data, and scikit-learn for prediction.
